record.title: ForFabSat: A Research Factory to Analyze Series Production for Networks of Small Satellites
record.abstract: The paradigm shift from traditional manufacturing of few satellites to hundreds of satellites for mega-constellations in low Earth orbits (LEO) poses new challenges for satellite design, development process and production in space industry. Increasing automation and the industrialization of manufacturing processes will play a key role here. This contribution summarizes the concepts and methods applied to implement related capabilities step by step in the research factory ForFabSat. Advanced industrial production methods of industry 4.0 and digital twins, as in automotive or consumer electronics mass markets, are adapted to the specifics of satellite production for hostile space environment. Here, in particular integration of time-consuming test procedures into the production process require special attention. Depending on targetted satellite quantities, different levels of cooperation between automation systems with robots and human workers are to be realized to be most cost-efficient. In ForFabSat capabilities are provided to analyze and compare for different production steps alternative approaches. In ForFabSat the technology readiness level (TRL) for satellite series production is planned to be increased from the current laboratory factory with implemented first exemplary integration and test cells at a TRL about 3 to an integrated research factory with TRL 5. A planned output capacity of more than 300 satellites per year will be realized through a sophisticated logistics concept including external suppliers. The research factory can be booked and accessed by industry as infrastructure via closed innovation cells, where companies can further analyze and optimize their specific products in crucial production steps . For implementation of future multi-satellite formations, in particular new tests related to the interaction between the satellites are to be included. Beyond traditional space environment tests (radiation, thermal vacuum cycling, vibrations, etc.) new challenges concern cooperative networked satellite system control, inter-satellite links, autonomous reaction capabilities, relative navigation, collision avoidance, etc.. Related hardware and software systems are to be characterized by hardware-in-the-loop-tests before launch. These aspects were already addressed in the NetSat formation mission (4 satellites; launched 2020) and are further expanded to current formations, such as CloudCT with 10 satellites self-organizing for joint observations of clouds for improved climate predictions.

record.title: Guidance and control for aerodynamic based nanosat multi-static SAR formation flying mission aimed at sub-milli-meter space debris characterization.
record.abstract: Low earth orbits (LEO) and very low earth orbits(VLEO) are important regions for space-based applications like Earth observation, Telecommunication, and Astrophysics. Understanding and modeling the Space debris in this region is of utmost importance for space situational awareness. Specifically, due to the limitations of ground-based sensor systems, the detection and characterization of sub-millimeter-level objects require an in-situ sensor system. In these regions, the effect of aerodynamic force is significant, as a result, utilization of this force for position control is very attractive, especially for nanosats. This will enable nanosats not to carry propulsion system leading to increased available size, weight, and power (SWAP) for mission outputs such as science data by increasing the payload quality and mission redundancy via extra sensors and actuators. In this work, we are proposing a guidance and control methodology for a novel aerodynamics-based nanosat formation flying mission. As the size and shape of the debris are not known a priori, the multi-static synthetic aperture radar (MSSAR) technique is considered to detect and characterize the sub-millimeter debris particles. The proposed guidance generates coupled translation and attitude trajectories that are optimized in terms of coverage area thereby increasing the detection and characterization of debris particles in different regions. Constraints specific to this mission such as maximum separation distance, position and attitude accuracy, and traditional constraints like collision avoidance are integrated into the guidance method. Moreover, the dynamics model includes co-rotation of the atmosphere with respect to earth, perturbation effects until the order smaller than aerodynamic forces $(O(10^{-5}\sim10^{-6}) m/s^2)$, for example until J3 for non-spherical effects. The controller considered is an adaptive controller that takes care of the model uncertainties and accounts for the errors coming from sensors and actuators. Furthermore, a learning-based polynomial density model is used for guidance. It utilizes the NRLMSISE-00 reference model and can adapt to new information. For the adaptive controller, a receding horizon-based estimator (RHE) estimates density with the latest available information. If the error exceeds a threshold, guidance trajectories are regenerated with updated information, ensuring the framework's robustness and reliability in changing environmental conditions. High-fidelity numerical simulation campaigns demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of the developed guidance and control methodology for different MSSAR formation flying configurations.

record.title: Building a Lightweight Data Management Tool for Small Satellite Missions
record.abstract: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) has received widespread adoption in the space industry, allowing engineers to develop, design and validate their activities through formal models. MBSE's perceived benefits include enhanced communication, complexity management, knowledge transfer, and improved verification capabilities through traceability. However, generic or tailored MBSE tools have not yet found such widespread adoption in small satellite missions, such as CubeSats. Drawing from a review of previous and current missions, we postulate that many MBSE tools and processes add a considerable overhead in terms of time, cost and effort to establish and maintain models. On the other hand, Document-Based Systems Engineering, often used on such projects, may suffer from inconsistency, lack of detail, and difficulty in accessing reliable and up-to-date engineering data. In this paper, we propose a concept and design for a new software tool for small spacecraft engineering, focused on engineering parameter management and sharing. This design is based on modern design and user experience principles, with a basic requirement of allowing users to access any engineering parameter within 20 seconds of having access to a web browser. The tool uses a standard block-based structure to describe the hierarchy of a space system, with modifiable parameters and content assigned to each block. This structure is stored under a version-controlled database (such as \emph{git} or \emph{dolt}), allowing history tracking, merging, auditing and real-time collaboration. Ready-made templates can also be used to produce aggregate values, such as mass or cost budgets. A REST API allows integration with different external tools, such as MS Excel Power Query, and an integration with an AI-based copilot is envisioned. To complement the design concept of our tool, we additionally provide User Interface mockups of key actions, as well as an early functional proof-of-concept developed with a Python backend. We use data from the POQUITO mission from the University of Luxembourg to emulate a use case in our proof-of-concept. This implementation is also released as free software to allow future users to modify and extend our tool. We conclude with a roadmap for the potential future development of the tool, with an aim of improving the engineering data management workflow for small satellite missions and surpass the limits of document-based information tracking, without the added burden of industrial modelling processes.

record.title: Architecture of a Simulation Test Bench for Operating Large Satellite Constellations
record.abstract: The approach of using FlatSats to aid the development and testing of a mission has been adopted effectively for CubeSats and small satellites. However, when considering a satellite constellation, the FlatSat approach can become limited, which is where simulating the interaction between the space and ground segments of large constellations offers a powerful enhancement. Moreover, such a simulation can be employed to evaluate new technologies and quantify their potential impact in the operation of a constellation. This paper presents an innovative architecture for a simulator designed to precisely meet these challenges.\\ The simulator deploys the NASA Operational Simulator for Small Satellites (NOS3), building on its heritage, open source components, active development and support. The use of NOS3 as the underlying simulation engine ensures compatibility with a wide range of hardware and software systems, which facilitates the testing and validation of satellite designs. It also allows for the incorporation of additional data sources and the emulation of hardware components, thereby contributing to the realism of the simulation.\\ Our proposed architecture addresses the challenges of simulating large satellite constellations, including scaling, computational efficiency and fidelity of the system modelling. A key feature of the simulator is its modularity, which allows for the integration of different flight software frameworks, subsystem models and ground segment software. These, in combination, permit different types of constellations to be simulated.\\ The simulator uses a fully containerized and microservice architecture, which ensures its portability and ease of deployment across different computing environments. This also facilitates the management of dependencies, isolation and rapid scaling of the simulation environment. Furthermore, the simulator can be run on a self-hosted infrastructure, providing users with full control over their simulation environment and data. This is particularly beneficial for organizations with strict data security requirements or those wishing to integrate the simulator into their existing infrastructure. Alternatively, the architecture can be easily deployed in a cloud-based infrastructure. The details of the design, its implementation, and its performance in several simulation scenarios will be presented.\\ We will also present how this architecture can be deployed as an operational simulator or as a test bench for new technologies, such as exploring the use of a Digital Twin in the operation of a satellite constellation.

record.title: F-Series: A Generic Development Kit for Intelligent Mini and Small Satellites
record.abstract: The ideology promoted about building NewSpace small satellites includes short development times and “off-the-shelf” parts for cost effectiveness. Already based on these criteria, a 120kg satellite named “Flying Laptop” was developed at the Stuttgart University in cooperation and guidance from Airbus. It was launched in 2017 and is still reliably operational, has three axis stabilization and uses off-the-shelf units. The development while fulfilling some main criteria also showed deficiencies. Until launch it took more than 7 years and scalability was achieved only for the software. Airbus from this baseline initiated a consortium with diverse SMEs in a continuous effort to optimize the ideology and technology about building satellites. Tenets of this “{\it F-Series}” approach include automotive-like Scrum development and continuous verification, scalable avionics, again employing “off-the-shelf” parts, a consistent path from early digital twin to full flight hardware/software/operations featuring flexible payload connectivity. Considering the main takeaways from diverse modelled satellites and studies, the {\it F-Series development kit} for building SmallSats emerged. Its key elements are \begin{itemize} \item hardware - the modular onboard computer and power units, sensors, actuators/propulsion, \item flight software – highly configurable w.r.t. satellite modes, orbits, single/multiple payload control, \item the digital twin (satellite simulator), \item intelligent payload subsystem and \item an operations suite featuring full encryption. \end{itemize} This paper will discuss each of these elements in detail. In order to refine the development time, the kit comes with an agile plan helping users eliminate any uncontrolled processes and reworks. It is based on {\it development benches} also being part of the kit. These benches – digital twins – are starting from a fully simulated satellite including the flight software source and provides connectivity to various mission control suites. After the SmallSat design having reached a certain development readiness, the hardware core avionics are available for seamless connection to the existing simulator replacing formerly simulated units. The process evolves up to the final satellite flight model. The {\it development kit} is usable both for CubeSats and SmallSats. By applying the same software and similar avionics and operations concept, the scaling of satellites becomes straightforward, permitting to keep all the supporting infrastructure and trained personnel. This paper cites CubeSat example missions like “EIVE” and the Swedish/German AI mission “ICE-Brain-1” and explains how such a development kit overcomes scalability challenges, and operational flexibility limits. Finally, the paper lists different SME partners of the {\it F-Series consortium} with shared ideologies.

record.title: Perception data system for satellite monitoring of strategic assets
record.abstract: Considering the different ways of applying nanosatellites, their inherent cost advantages, and the fact that this field represents a strategic area, the development of the Perception system for data collection via satellite is proposed. The Perception is a system for monitoring and producing strategic assets that uses the CubeSat standard as an instrument for the transition from scientific research to the product of technological innovation for sustainable development. Specifically, we aim to create a concept of operation, bringing the digital twin approach to deliver, among others, a new small satellite simulation environment based on the hardware-in-the-loop concept integrating the STK software, Helmholtz cage, air bearing top tables, and a flat satellite with an SDR payload for store-and-forward applications. The expected outcomes include a structured engineering model to define and validate the architecture of complex systems based on the CubeSat standard. The pilot project is aimed at collecting data via satellite from the K34 Tower of the Large-Scale Biosphere-Atmosphere Program in the Amazon (LBA), whose data is used to monitor carbon flow, among other applications. The K34 Tower is in the Amazon rainforest, approximately 64km from Manaus city, Brazil. Applications aimed at tracking unmanned aerial vehicles that support environmental monitoring activities will also be considered. Moreover, the restructuring of the entire Laboratory of Simulation and Control of Aerospace Systems, LODESTAR, at the University of Brasília is being guided by the concepts and methods of the Perception system, seeking to innovatively integrate the digital twin concept into its new physical and logical architecture. This work presents an overview of the Perception data system, its main architectures and systems, and future contributions.

record.title: Sounding Balloons as a Low-Cost Platform for CubeSat Subsystem Validation: Insights from the Cloudview Missions
record.abstract: Testing CubeSat subsystems in relevant environments before launch is challenging due to cost and accessibility constraints. Sounding balloons provide a low-cost, high-altitude alternative for validating hardware and software in near-space conditions, offering a practical stepping stone for mission readiness. This paper examines the use of sounding balloons as a CubeSat subsystem test platform, using the Cloudview series of missions as a case study. Cloudview-01, launched in 2023, demonstrated the feasibility of testing avionics, onboard image processing, and passive thermal control at high altitude. It also highlighted key limitations, including the failure of the commercial Tracking, Telemetry, and Command (TT\&C) module and the need for better thermal regulation. These findings informed the design of Cloudview-02, launching in June 2025, which expands the methodology with an active thermal control system, a new TT\&C subsystem, a CubeSat chassis, and an antenna deployment testbed. Additionally, Cloudview-02 will validate a custom image compression algorithm, building on the segmentation algorithm successfully tested in Cloudview-01 (see IAC-24, B1, IP, 157, "AI-Based Wildfire Risk Assessment from Low-Cost Multispectral Data: Collection, Processing, and Analysis for Sub-6U CubeSat Missions"). Beyond specific hardware tests, the missions have refined engineering workflows, integrating Agile methodologies and model-based systems engineering (MBSE) to address the challenges of student-led development. A balloon trajectory simulator, validated against real flight data, has further improved mission planning and risk mitigation. These missions are conducted by GU Orbit, the University of Glasgow’s student-led CubeSat society, which provides students with hands-on experience in satellite engineering, mission design, and space systems development. Operating within the constraints of high student turnover and limited funding, GU Orbit has adapted industry-standard processes such as MBSE to maintain consistency across projects and ensure that lessons learned are effectively passed down to future teams. The Cloudview program serves as a proving ground for iterative, low-cost CubeSat subsystem testing, bridging the gap between academic research and practical mission development. The results of these flights reinforce the viability of sounding balloons as a low-cost CubeSat testing platform, providing rapid iteration cycles and high-altitude conditions that approximate aspects of the space environment. Lessons from Cloudview-02 will inform future subsystem testing campaigns, supporting a structured, scalable approach for CubeSat development.

record.title: The Circle: Future Earth Observation System Architecture System of Systems Analysis from a Science Need Perspective
record.abstract: "The Circle" is an ESA project which aims to create a science-driven Earth Observation (EO) reference architecture. This project addresses critical scientific questions from the European Space Agency's (ESA) Science strategy, leveraging the full potential of the EO ecosystem. It is thus meant to explore the future architecture of EO systems, aiming to enhance the digital presence and customer engagement of the ESA. The primary goal is to investigate new domains of EO based on scientific needs, using a system-of-systems (SoS) approach and empowering innovative techniques for evaluating systems architectures while contextually employing analyses regarding complementarity economies and industrial policies. This approach considers the entire EO ecosystem, including satellite fleets, in-situ data, high-altitude pseudo-satellites (HAPS), and digital infrastructure, to address key scientific questions. The study involves developing a new EO reference architecture that includes various components such as user-stakeholder needs, operational and scientific satellite components, commercial and small satellite components, data and operations management, access to space, ground segment, technical and industrial components, predictive modeling, and international partnerships. The project addresses five main scientific questions: 1. How has the ocean carbon cycle responded to anthropogenic CO2 and climate change? 2. What are the key drivers for the mass balance change of ice sheets, ice shelves, and glaciers? 3. Where and how are ecosystems undergoing critical transitions? 4. How has the land biosphere responded to human activity and climate change? 5. How important are anthropogenic influences on the water cycle, and how accurately can we predict them? The Circle aims to develop a new EO reference architecture with components such as user-stakeholder needs, operational and scientific satellite components, commercial and small satellite components, data and operations management, and international partnerships. The project involves six main tasks: • Understanding the status and future plans for the ESA EO Reference Architecture. • Analyzing the observation and measurement requirements needed to address the scientific questions introduced above. • Developing baseline EO and SoS scenarios for these questions, considering different timelines. • Conducting SoS analyses for future scenarios to address the scientific questions and design an EO ecosystem for 2050+. • Analyzing the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of different future scenarios and developing an action plan. The Circle aims to create a sustainable, living EO ecosystem that continuously evolves to meet user needs, with a strategic vision targeting beyond 2050 and intermediate steps planned for 2030 and 2040.

record.title: Maintenance and sustainability in orbit: modular standard for the new generation of satellites
record.abstract: The increasing reliance on satellites for scientific, commercial and defense applications require a paradigm shift in design and maintenance strategies. In particular, current CubeSat architectures lack structure modularity to make in-orbit repairs and upgrades. This paper proposes a standardized modular construction protocol for CubeSats, allowing for component replacement and maintenance directly in space. The proposed structure envisages CubeSats as interconnected functional modules, facilitating the removal of damaged units and the integration of upgraded components, thus extending mission duration and reducing space debris. This paper outlines the development of a universally accepted standard for the modular assembly of CubeSats that requires international collaboration between space agencies, industry players and research institutes. This protocol will enable interoperability between modules from different manufacturers and nations by defining uniform physical and communication interfaces. The framework could also serve as a basis for future applications in larger spacecraft, supporting the evolution of in-space manufacturing and in-orbit servicing. To reach the aim of this paper, a Model-Based System Engineering approach is pursued. This study is carried out in the framework of the Space Exploration and Development Systems XVII (SEEDS XVII) II Level Master’s programme, a project born from the collaboration between the Politecnico di Torino (PoliTo), the Institut Supérieur de l’Aèronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE) and the University of Leicester, with the participation of Agenzia Spaziale Italiana (ASI), Centre National D’Etudes Spatiales (CNES), European Space Agency (ESA), Thales Alenia Space and Altec.

record.title: Advancing CubeSat Reliability: A Model-Based Systems Engineering Approach for Fault-Tolerant, Real-Time Software
record.abstract: The University of Würzburg Experimental Satellite 5 (UWE-5) mission is advancing model-based systems engineering methodologies through the development of a modular, real-time capable on-board software framework. Designed for operation within a lightweight 128KB memory footprint, this framework integrates formalized system modeling, fault-tolerant architectures, and dynamic resource management, enabling CubeSat missions to autonomously maintain critical functions under under strict power and computational constraints. Rather than relying solely on failure recovery, the system employs proactive fault prevention to enhance mission reliability.\\ To ensure robustness, the software framework follows a digital engineering approach, incorporating modeling and simulation for early-stage validation. By leveraging FreeRTOS as a deterministic execution model, it enforces predictable task scheduling while a structured task hierarchy and adaptive task state management optimize real-time execution. These features align with modern system engineering (SE) modeling techniques, allowing for systematic performance analysis across multiple operational scenarios.\\ The framework undergoes rigorous validation and verification using a combination of hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) and software-in-the-loop (SIL) simulations, digital twin analysis, and subsystem-level testing. Initial tests confirm that hardware load limitations effectively prevent instability, while upcoming power consumption evaluations will assess the system’s ability to dynamically adapt energy usage. These validation steps represent a transition from ad hoc CubeSat software engineering to a structured, model-driven approach, ensuring improved reliability and scalability for future missions.\\ By integrating model-based verification, simulation-driven validation, and structured fault management, this work contributes to next-generation SE modeling practices that enhance mission resilience and reduce risks and costs. The structured approach moves beyond reactive software development, incorporating proactive fault detection, dynamic resource allocation, and modular task management to ensure robust execution even in resource-constrained environments. The lessons learned from this development provide valuable insights into scalable software architectures for CubeSat missions, demonstrating how a well-structured SE modeling approach can improve system reliability, maintainability, and performance.\\ This framework as part of the UWE-5 mission serves as a proof of concept for integrating SE modeling techniques into small satellite software engineering, laying the groundwork for future advancements in digital system design.

record.title: AI-Driven Fault Detection and Recovery in CubeSat Constellations for Autonomous Space Networking
record.abstract: \documentclass{article} \begin{document} \title{AI-Driven Fault Detection and Recovery in CubeSat Constellations for Autonomous Space Networking} \maketitle \begin{abstract} The increasing deployment of CubeSat constellations for Earth observation, communication, and scientific missions introduces challenges related to fault detection, network resilience, and autonomous recovery. Traditional fault management techniques rely on ground-based diagnostics, resulting in delays and inefficiencies. This study presents an AI-driven approach for real-time fault detection and autonomous recovery in CubeSat constellations, leveraging machine learning (ML) models trained on telemetry data to predict and mitigate anomalies before critical failures occur. Our proposed framework utilizes deep learning-based anomaly detection to identify deviations in satellite health parameters, such as power fluctuations, thermal anomalies, and communication disruptions. Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms further enable dynamic fault mitigation strategies by autonomously reconfiguring network paths and redistributing workloads among operational CubeSats. By implementing federated learning, our system ensures decentralized AI model updates across the constellation without excessive data transmission to ground stations, preserving bandwidth and enhancing security. Simulations conducted using digital twin models of CubeSat networks demonstrate an improvement in fault recovery time by up to 40\%, along with a 30\% reduction in communication latency compared to conventional fault-handling approaches. The ability to autonomously predict and respond to system failures significantly enhances the resilience and longevity of CubeSat networks, making them more viable for long-term space applications. This work aligns with the IAC 2025 theme, "Sustainable Space: Resilient Earth," by contributing to the development of robust, autonomous, and scalable small satellite architectures. The proposed AI-based fault management system paves the way for more intelligent, adaptive, and cost-effective CubeSat constellations, reducing mission downtime and operational risks in future space-based networks. \textbf{Keywords:} AI in space, CubeSat constellations, fault detection, reinforcement learning, anomaly detection, federated learning, autonomous networking. \end{abstract} \end{document}

record.title: In-situ Power System Modeling for Micro/Nano Satellite Autonomous Operation System
record.abstract: This paper discusses the battery parameter and status estimation utilizing multiple satellite operational data to achieve efficient autonomous operations. There are two main purposes for our trials: one is the establishment of an autonomous operational planning simulator with suitable accuracy, computational cost, and maintenance abilities. The other is the establishment of the on-board status and parameter estimator resulting in suitable accuracies. Autonomous operations are a key technology for mega-constellations construction avoiding human error, instability in quality, and reduce enormous human resources. The automation techniques require evaluation index. Here, we set efficiency and safety in operation planning as evaluation index to maximize the mission achievement because the micro/nano satellites have severe mass and volume limitation. Here, we are proposing operational planning system focusing on the power consumption ratio: bus operation to the maximum power generation, which switches the optimization methods based on the ratio. The proposed system uses the battery charging status as constraints for optimization. Therefore, the proposed system has to estimate exact battery status and be tuned the system model parameters following the actual spacecraft status data. In addition, the spacecraft also has to mount on-board realtime battery status estimator to utilize the planned mission profile safety. In the proposed system, we set the equivalent circuit model constructed with multiple spacecraft parameters for the battery status simulation. The spacecraft parameters, such as battery internal resistance, tend to vary by aging or environmental effects. Therefore, the parameters have to mount the ability to update the system parameters immediately using the actual measurement data of the spacecraft. This paper compares battery simulators parameters determined from the ground test with those from the actual operation data of 1U CubeSat and 50kg-size satellites. In addition, the parameter variation effects for the battery status estimation results are also discussed. For the parameter estimation methods, we apply the alternating-current impedance method to the ground test data, and apply logarithmic parameter estimation that uses the unscented Kalman filter to actual operation data. The results show there are some differences in the estimated parameters depending on the applied data, and the estimation methods. In addition, we demonstrate the effects of the parameter’s variations for the operational planner or simulators and compare the results with actual operational data.

record.title: Enabling Resilient disaster managment and precision agriculture through VLEO Earth observation constellation
record.abstract: Very Low Earth Orbits (VLEO), defined as altitudes below 450 km, are gaining renewed interest in the commercial space sector, particularly for Earth observation (EO) and communication applications. The ability to operate at lower altitudes provides significant advantages to spacecraft design, including higher spatial resolution in imaging, reduced latency in communications with improved link budgets, a reduction in overall mass, and a benevolent space atmosphere. The use of less powerful payloads, while maintaining LEO-type payload performance, makes VLEO-EO cost-effective and efficient as compared to the state-of-the-art LEO. Additionally, VLEO satellites are inherently more sustainable than higher-altitude satellites, as they are self-cleaning by naturally deorbiting due to aerodynamic drag, preventing further accumulation of space debris. These benefits make VLEO-EO satellites particularly relevant for sustainability-driven applications, such as rapid disaster management and sustainable agriculture. To fully take advantage of VLEO-EO, novel mission concepts and integration with influential emerging trends like edge computing and in-orbit refueling must be explored. This study investigates how VLEO EO satellites can support two key sustainability topics: disaster response and precision agriculture. Rapid imaging capabilities from VLEO can significantly improve situational awareness during natural disasters, while high-resolution, multi-modal sensing can enhance crop monitoring and resource management, enabling climate resilience in agriculture. To evaluate the feasibility of VLEO EO for these focused applications, system models were developed for multiple payload types, including hyperspectral, thermal infrared, LiDAR, and very high-resolution optical sensors. System-level models were used to propose potential satellite designs by taking case studies for particular applications. The study also explores the integration of emerging technologies such as edge computing, which enables real-time data processing, methods for compensating atmospheric drag and in-orbit refueling for extending mission lifetime, and reducing the wet mass of satellites. The study also investigated challenges, including atmospheric drag, limited orbital lifetimes, the need for advanced propulsion, and control strategies to offer a comprehensive system model for satellites with the aforementioned emerging trends. Findings indicate that VLEO EO satellites present significant advantages for sustainability-focused applications, offering enhanced spatial resolution, improved revisit times, and cost-effective mission architectures. The integration of edge computing reduces dependence on ground stations. It allows for faster decision-making, while in-orbit servicing and aerodynamic control strategies mitigate the primary limitations of VLEO, such as orbital decay and propellant constraints. These advancements enable a new generation of agile, cost-efficient EO missions that are highly responsive to both environmental and societal needs.

record.title: Digital Twin Technology for Small Satellite Development and Operations: A Case Study of HEAD-2D
record.abstract: Abstract—With the development of modern small satellite technology, satellites play more and more important roles in remote sensing, broadband communication, navigation and scientific research. In recent years, the large-scale constellation plans are put forward continuously, SpaceX, Oneweb and Amazon have announced their large-scale broadband internet satellite constellations. Stimulate by commercial capital and market, the satellite industry develops fast. Low cost, short development cycle, digitalization, networking and intelligence become its trend. The mode of design, manufacture and operation of satellites (constellations) need to change at the same time. Digital Twin is a cutting-edge technology that has revolutionized the industry by mirroring almost every facet of a product, process, or service. It has the potential to replicate spacecraft in the physical world in the digital space and provide developers with feedback from the virtual world. As a result, the technology enables developers to quickly detect and solve physical problems, design and build better spacecrafts, and realize value and benefits faster than previously possible. Furthermore, the Digital Twin technology helps to improve the development processes and performance of small satellites. In this article, we developed a digital twin system for the small satellite HEAD-2D, the digital twin system consisted of satellite models, database, running environment and communication interfaces between the digital twin and the physical satellite. The digital models are developed using C# and Creo tools. Based on the digital twin system, we could simulate the operation state of HEAD-2D satellite in orbit by configuring parameters and status. With the digital twin, it is easy to optimize and estimate the operation state and sytem design. For new missions, we could build the digital twin of the new missions and evaluate the technology feasibility by configure corresponding parameters. The digital twin is also useful for new staffs to learn the composition and principle of satellites.

record.title: Integrating Concurrent Engineering with Data-Driven and Model-Based Systems Engineering for End-to-End Small-Satellite Design
record.abstract: Concurrent Engineering (CE) is a collaborative product development approach that emphasizes the parallelization of tasks, and integrates design with other crucial tasks, such as manufacturing planning, quality assurance, and serviceability, to accelerate development, reduce costs, and improve quality. The current application of CE facilitates the reduction of timelines and enhances communication among the various disciplines involved, addressing the complexities of mission analysis and feasibility phases (Phase 0 and Phase A) in space projects, with some application up to Phase B. However, its full potential is still to be disclosed, to cover the full product lifecycle until the disposal phase. To support this extension of applicability, a critical challenge of the concurrent design approach needs first to be overcome: the seamless integration across organizational borders due to both technical limitations in data exchange systems and the inherent complexity of space systems. Achieving full compatibility between diverse systems and real-time data synchronization remains difficult, primarily due to tool, standard, and process variations across different partners. To address these challenges, an integration of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and Data-Driven Systems Engineering (DDSE) has been proposed to further enhance the concurrent design process. While MBSE provides structured modeling for system behavior and requirements management, the introduction of DDSE enables data-driven decision-making and ensures continuous information flow across all phases of the mission. By combining these methodologies, we propose an integrated and agile approach that maintains a single source of truth, ensures continuity of information across the mission lifecycle, and facilitates collaboration among engineering teams and stakeholders. The integrated approach is currently being successfully applied to small satellite missions and systems design, covering a wide variety of mission concepts from LEO Earth Observation missions to close-proximity operations missions, up to deep-space missions, with a focus to the CubeSat platform. The paper aims to first present the methodology and the integration of tools and subsequently present the result from a case study, showcasing how the efficiency and effectiveness of design and decision-making processes have been improved. This methodology demonstrates how CE, when combined with MBSE and DDSE, can optimize space mission design from concept to manufacturing and testing up to in-orbit operations and disposal, providing a robust solution for small satellite and space systems development.

record.title: Validation of Alba CubeSat’s Thermal Model: from simulations to experimental testing
record.abstract: Thermal modelling is a critical aspect of spacecraft design, ensuring components operate within safe temperature limits in the harsh environment of space. This paper presents a case study on the validation of the thermal model for the student project Alba CubeSat from the University of Padova. AlbaSat is a 2U CubeSat entirely developed by student which participated in the Fly Your Satellite! Design Booster programme in 2024 and was supported by ESA during the development of its satellite design. The team has now been selected for the ESA Fly Your Satellite! Test Opportunity programme which ensures the chance to conduct thermal tests at ESA’s facilities “ESEC-Galaxia” in Belgium allowing the students to test the CubeSat’s thermal performance in a thermal vacuum chamber (TVAC). This opportunity enables the comparison of results with those from thermal analyses and the validation the thermal model through the creation of a digital twin. The paper provides a detailed description of the Structural-Thermal Model (STM) developed by the students to ensure an accurate representation of the CubeSat’s thermal behaviour. It outlines the setup and methodology of the thermal analyses conducted using the Radian Systems software, highlighting the specific configurations and assumptions made during the simulations. The mathematical results will be compared with the data collected by the thermocouples during thermal balance procedure to understand which assumptions worked and which parameters could be further improved to obtain even more reliable results A key aspect of this research is its educational value. The entire process, from analysis to testing and validation, is carried out by students, offering hands-on experience in spacecraft thermal application.

record.title: Assessment of the Realization of Value and Benefits of Implementing Agile MBSE for Enterprises in the NewSpace Industry
record.abstract: In the fast-paced landscape of technology and innovation, achieving safety and rapid market delivery necessitates the quantification of digital resources to minimize risks and enhance the maturity level of technology and product development. Among established space agencies, MBSE maturity has been achieved through decades of customized and integrated practices, leveraging multiple tools and synchronized techniques. However, implementing MBSE in small satellite missions, such as CubeSat projects, presents challenges for university developers and start-up owners due to resource constraints. In the NewSpace ecosystem, where the demand for agile digital engineering is increasing, MBSE must be applied in a targeted, flexible, and effective manner. Prior research highlights that MBSE’s comprehensive nature can limit agile attributes, which are critical for small teams and emerging enterprises. Our previous work proposes an objective-driven approach that aligns the lifecycle stage with core MBSE processes and activities. These phases serve as anchors for MBSE implementation, ensuring a structured framework that defines the objectives and scope of the model, facilitating measurable, achievable, and quantifiable applications. Additionally, the incremental nature of Agile, combined with the digital thread of MBSE artifacts, will be analyzed to establish metrics that evaluate digital engineering efforts against target objectives. This hybrid approach breaks down the MBSE process into measurable steps, providing indicators of sufficient system information to support decision-makers throughout the concept, production, space deployment, and operational phases. To maximize the utility of MBSE artifacts, a metric-driven modeling approach will align efforts with critical decision-making milestones. The inclusion of project managers, quality management, procurement, and production teams in the planning process is essential to achieving optimal results. However, these metrics may not serve as a one-size-fits-all solution, but rather as an effective organizational tool to meet stakeholder needs and ensure maximum utilization of technical resources. This study investigates whether Agile MBSE implementation, within organizational strategies, effectively meets the demands of the NewSpace industry by supporting both technical and operational frameworks. The assessment underscores the transformative potential of Agile MBSE, positioning it as a key methodology for evolving the NewSpace industry and enhancing enterprise-level digital engineering.

record.title: AI4CE Update: A Comparative Study of AI-based CubeSat Design Generation Against Real-World Systems
record.abstract: The current progress of the AI4CE system is presented, an open-source tool developed for the automated generation of conceptual space system designs, with an initial focus on CubeSat configurations. Designed to benchmark AI-based methods against conventional approaches, the tool utilizes Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to rapidly synthesize design solutions within a Concurrent Engineering (CE) framework. To facilitate integration with established Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) environments, the generated designs are directly exported into an ECSS 10-25 compliant COMET model and SysMLv2 format. The primary objective of the work is to investigate the feasibility and potential benefits of using DRL to generate complete satellite designs and to determine whether an AI-driven process can offer advantages over traditional design methodologies. Several challenges inherent to CubeSat system design are addressed, including multidimensional optimization, a vast combinatorial design space, varying subsystem complexities, and the formulation of multiple constraints. A composite evaluation function has been employed to quantitatively assess each generated design based on the degree of requirement fulfillment, along with secondary metrics such as mass, cost, and power consumption. It is hypothesized that a design which satisfies a higher number of mission-specific requirements—and excels in additional performance parameters—demonstrates the high potential impact of AI-based system generation in accelerating CE studies. A case study based on the OPS-Sat mission is detailed, wherein a requirements report was used to drive the system generation process. A pre-trained Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent was tasked with generating a CubeSat design from a comprehensive database of available components. The resulting design was then systematically compared with an existing, real-world configuration by evaluating the fulfillment of requirements and additional performance criteria. Preliminary results indicate that design iteration times have been reduced from hours or days to mere minutes, thereby enabling rapid exploration and refinement of diverse design alternatives. Planned future developments include the expansion of the component database, the refinement of DRL algorithms, and the integration of alternative static optimizers to further enhance the system’s performance. In addition, the versatility of the approach is expected to extend its applicability beyond CubeSats to other modular systems such as drones, rovers, tiny houses, space stations, and ground segments. The implementation of AI-driven system generation, as demonstrated by AI4CE, is anticipated to contribute significantly to the democratization of space system design and to accelerate the overall system engineering process by enabling faster, more efficient, and innovative design solutions. For more information about AI4CE: https://ai4ce.space

record.title: An Advanced Simulation Framework for Sail-Driven Spacecraft Dynamics and Control
record.abstract: The development of spacecrafts with solar and drag sails has gained significant interest in recent years due to their potential for fuel-free propulsion and extended mission lifetimes. This paper begins with a study of current space missions that utilize sail-driven technology, highlighting their applications, challenges, and technological advancements. Based on this analysis, we emphasize the necessity of an accurate and efficient simulation environment for testing and validating control systems designed for solar and drag sail spacecraft, particularly in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), where atmospheric drag plays a crucial role in the disturbance forces. To address this need, we present the implementation of the Drag Deorbit Device (D3) in a CubeSat platform, a propellant-less deployable and controllable drag sail system. Additionally, we propose an advanced Software-in-the-Loop (SIL) simulation framework that overcomes the limitations of previous simulation tools. The presented approach integrates Isaac Sim and Robot Operating System (ROS), leveraging the advantages of physics-based real-time simulation, high-fidelity rendering, and seamless hardware integration. In addition, enhanced GPU-accelerated physics for precise force and torque modeling, modular extensibility for integrating custom spacecraft dynamics, and real-time visualization for intuitive debugging and system analysis is considered. The presented simulation system incorporates orbital perturbations such as gravity gradient effects, atmospheric drag, gravitational anomalies, and forces from relative motion in an elliptical orbit, providing a more realistic operational environment. Instead of relying on predefined mass distribution, this approach applies drag forces directly on the spacecraft’s surface, leveraging the physics engine to naturally resolve the resulting dynamics while maintaining accuracy and enabling seamless adaptation to different spacecraft designs. The proposed SIL architecture follows a digital twin paradigm, ensuring a high-fidelity representation of the spacecraft’s dynamics and control systems within the virtual environment. This digital twin enables rapid prototyping, real-time testing, and iterative refinement of control strategies before deployment in space. By bridging the gap between simulation and real-world implementation, the presented system significantly enhances the reliability and robustness of solar sail spacecraft operations. Through this work, we demonstrate the reliability and accuracy of the proposed system using real data, validating its effectiveness for spacecraft simulation and control in LEO. Additionally, we analyze deorbiting maneuvers to assess the system’s performance in end-of-mission scenarios.

record.title: L1 Optical Lensing (LOL): Using the Earth as an Atmospheric Lens
record.abstract: The Terrascope concept has been firstly introduced by D. Kipping in 2019, and it has increasingly gained scientific attention. This concept uses a satellite at Lagrange point 1 and involves using Earth's atmosphere as a lens to amplify light from distant astronomical bodies. If successful, the Terrascope could revolutionize deep space observation by enhancing angular resolution and amplification. Indeed, in previous studies, D. Kipping determined an estimated amplification of order 22,500: the computed amplification decreased after accounting for the effects of turbulence, absorption, transmission, and scattering of Earth’s atmosphere, and the estimated image reconstruction has been performed taking into account Earth’s oblateness. \\ On these premises, 'L1 Optical Lensing (LOL.)' mission is carried out and aims to characterize the amplification and the resolution of the Terrascope concept by using a satellite placed at a Hill radius distance from Earth, serving both as a technological and scientific demonstration. This study was initially conducted during ESA’s CubeSat Summer School 2024 in ESEC using a Model-Based Systems Engineering approach with the COMET tool and ESA expert support. The proposed satellite would be launched as a secondary payload on the Ariane 62 rocket in 2030, alongside ESA's NEOMIR mission. The first presented system analysis resulted in a 12U CubeSat design at both system and subsystem level, including system budgets and subsystem analyses. The optical payload consisted of visible and infrared detectors aiming to observe distant celestial objects in the anti-sun direction such as high-redshift objects, active galactic nuclei, radio galaxies and exoplanets. In the subsequent iterations, the scale-up to a micro-satellite has emerged as the optimal solution due to payload constraints. In particular, a tailored payload ray-tracing design combined with AOCS fine guidance logic has been investigated. \\ Additionally, from a cost perspective, the main benefit of this concept is that it tackles the crisis in astronomy of making ever-larger space and ground-based telescopes. For instance, the upcoming Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) has an aperture diameter of 39 m and comes at a cost of 1.4B. Studies from D. Kipping predicted that a Terrascope of 1 m aperture diameter, placed at a Hill radius distance from Earth, could achieve the same amplification as a 150 m telescope on Earth, which would cost 50-100B. Therefore, using natural lensing instead of building ever-growing apertures could lead to comparable results in deep-space observation, at a fraction of the cost.

record.title: A Cyber-Functional Architecture Framework for Space Systems: Balancing Security and Mission Success
record.abstract: As space systems become increasingly interconnected and reliant on digital infrastructure, the need for robust cybersecurity frameworks and standards has never been more critical. Recent calls for unified cyber standards for space systems underscore the urgency of establishing clear, actionable guidelines for securing these assets. However, beyond defining standards, it is equally important to develop methods for assessing their implementation to evaluate whether a given space cybersecurity architecture is truly "good" at providing appropriate security for a given mission. This paper addresses the fundamental challenge of evaluating the cybersecurity posture of space system architectures, proposing an approach that balances mission success and cyber resilience. Specifically, we explore how a functional architecture for cybersecurity—one that is implementation-agnostic—can be developed to provide a structured approach for analysis and assessment. Our concept builds on established design patterns in both space system and cybersecurity domains. Space system patterns include the NASA Space Mission Architecture Framework, Human Spaceflight Reference Models, and CubeSat standards, while cybersecurity patterns encompass defense-in-depth, zero trust architectures, network segmentation, and fault-tolerant design. By integrating these frameworks, the proposed cyber-functional architecture framework enables a holistic assessment of space system architectures from a security perspective. Key to this approach is avoiding the pitfalls of some standards initiatives, where compliance criteria remain ambiguous and difficult to assess. Instead, we aim to provide tangible methods and tools for evaluating the balance of cybersecurity measures against mission requirements and operational constraints. This includes developing metrics, criteria, and tools for assessing compliance with cyber-functional design principles. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach by assessing Level 3 and 4 requirements for a representative space mission using the proposed methods. By aligning cybersecurity architecture patterns with mission-driven space system architectures, we propose a framework that ensures security is treated as a foundational design principle rather than a compliance afterthought.

record.title: Demonstration of an automated operation planning system for ONGLAISAT CubeSat
record.abstract: The ONGLAISAT CubeSat, developed through collaboration between the Taiwan Space Agency (TASA) and the University of Tokyo's Intelligent Space Systems Laboratory (ISSL), is designed to demonstrate high-resolution Earth observation using Time Delay Integration (TDI) technology. Given the limited human resources for operating small satellites, efficient automated operations are crucial. To address this, we developed an automated operation planning system for ONGLAISAT to automatically generate operation plans. The system operates in four main steps. First, the user inputs the operational goals, such as the images to be captured or the timing for data downlink. Second, an initial plan is generated through a state-space search using a simplified domain model, enabling quick solutions by omitting detailed physical quantities like power consumption or satellite attitude. Third, this plan is validated through high-fidelity simulations, where physical constraints and system behavior are accurately modeled. Any issues in the plan are identified during this validation phase. Finally, if the plan is deemed invalid, the system employs plan-space search to iteratively refine the plan until a valid solution is obtained. Feedback from the validation phase helps guide the search, with flaws evaluated using a heuristic function to determine the most efficient repair strategies. This approach ensures that the final plan successfully achieves the goals and is safely executable. Traditional automated planning systems often rely on rule-based approaches, which follow predefined rules to generate plans, limiting their flexibility. These rule-based systems cannot adapt to unforeseen situations. In contrast, our system employs model-based planning, which generates plans by dynamically adjusting based on the satellite's domain model. Additionally, by integrating high-fidelity simulations, the system generates reliable plans that can address a wide range of operational scenarios. This system was successfully demonstrated during ONGLAISAT's mission. It automatically generated operational plans, with their feasibility guaranteed through simulations, for tasks such as imaging and data downlink. These plans were executed on orbit, achieving the operational goals as planned. The feasibility of the operational plans was confirmed through this on-orbit demonstration, and the plan generation process proved both efficient and reliable, ensuring that the mission objectives were successfully met. This research demonstrates the feasibility of automating operation plan generation for CubeSats, improving efficiency and reliability while reducing human intervention and errors. The system provides a robust framework for automated satellite operation planning and can be applied to future, more complex missions.

record.title: Model-Based Systems Engineering approach in Capella for Concept of Operations and Operating Modes: Methodology comparison across space systems domains
record.abstract: In recent years, it has become more and more evident how Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) has emerged as a key approach to managing system complexity and ensuring rigorous traceability throughout the lifecycle of a system. When working particularly in highly constrained and mission-critical domains such as space exploration - where a high number of stakeholders and actors are to be involved and/or updated on various aspects - MBSE plays a vital role in enhancing system consistency, collaboration, and validation. This paper focuses on modeling the Concept of Operations (ConOps) and Operating Modes using Capella - an MBSE tool widely used by space domain actors. This work emphasizes their role in defining system behavior and mission scenarios from the early design stages. ConOps and Operating Modes form the backbone of mission planning, enabling engineers to foresee system responses under nominal and non-nominal conditions, optimize resource allocation, and improve system resilience. We present a methodology comparison for defining and modeling ConOps and Operating Modes within the MBSE framework, where flexibility is the key to adapting to different mission architectures and dynamic operational constraints. Our approach application is illustrated through two different case studies - a lunar habitat and a small-satellite - showing how MBSE can be leveraged to develop robust, adaptable, mission-ready systems. Through these examples, the benefits of integrating ConOps and Operating Modes early in the design phase are highlighted, improving decision-making, requirements validation, and mission assurance. The paper concludes with a discussion of the scalability of the approach and potential advances of MBSE methodologies for future space exploration missions.
